subject: science
title: KS3 / Year 7-9 Science — Physics: Space Reading
subtitle: Reading comprehension passages for KS3 physics space.
description: Reading passages and comprehension questions covering the Solar System, gravity, seasons, Moon phases, satellites, scale, exploration and working scientifically. The passages use English for both source and target text because this is a non-language science pack.

data.sourceTitle: The Solar System And Its Objects
data.targetTitle: The Solar System And Its Objects
data.sourcePassage: The Solar System is the Sun and all the objects held by the Sun's gravity. The Sun is a star, not a planet, and it contains most of the mass of the Solar System. Eight main planets orbit the Sun in the order Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus and Neptune. Smaller objects also belong to the Solar System. Asteroids are rocky bodies, many of them found between Mars and Jupiter. Comets are icy bodies that may form tails near the Sun and often follow stretched elliptical paths. Pluto is not one of the eight main planets because it is classed as a dwarf planet.

questions.question: What object is at the centre of the Solar System?
questions.modelAnswer: The Sun is at the centre of the Solar System.

questions.question: Which planet comes immediately after Earth in order from the Sun?
questions.modelAnswer: Mars comes immediately after Earth.

questions.question: Why is Pluto not listed as one of the eight main planets?
questions.modelAnswer: Pluto is classed as a dwarf planet because it has not cleared its orbital path.

questions.question: Explain one difference between an asteroid and a comet.
questions.modelAnswer: An asteroid is rocky, while a comet is icy and may form a tail near the Sun.

questions.question: What common film idea about the asteroid belt does the source correct?
questions.modelAnswer: It corrects the idea that the asteroid belt is tightly packed; the distances between objects are usually very large.

data.sourcePassage: Gravity is a non-contact force of attraction between objects with mass. The Sun has a very large mass, so its gravity controls the motion of planets. An orbit happens because an object moves forwards while gravity pulls it towards a larger body. Without gravity, the object would move off in a straight line. Without forward motion, it would fall directly inwards. With both forward motion and inward gravitational pull, the path curves and repeats. Astronauts in orbit feel weightless, but this does not mean there is no gravity. They float because they and their spacecraft are falling around Earth together.

questions.question: What type of force is gravity?
questions.modelAnswer: Gravity is a non-contact force of attraction between masses.

questions.question: What would happen to an orbiting object if there were no gravity?
questions.modelAnswer: It would move off in a straight line.
acceptedKeywords: It would move off in a straight line
options: It would move off in a straight line

questions.question: Why does Earth not fall straight into the Sun?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth has forward motion as well as being pulled inward by the Sun's gravity.

questions.question: Explain why astronauts can float even though gravity still acts on them.
questions.modelAnswer: Astronauts and their spacecraft are both falling around Earth together, so they feel weightless while gravity still pulls them.

questions.question: Why are many KS3 orbit diagrams simplified?
questions.modelAnswer: They often draw orbits as circles even though real orbits can be elliptical, so the diagram makes the idea easier but less accurate.

data.sourcePassage: Earth rotates on its axis once in about 24 hours, causing day and night. The side facing the Sun has daylight, while the side facing away has night. Earth also orbits the Sun once in about 365.25 days, which is one year. Seasons are not mainly caused by Earth being closer to or farther from the Sun. They are caused by Earth's tilted axis. When the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun, the UK receives more direct sunlight and longer daylight hours, so it has summer. When it is tilted away, sunlight is less direct and days are shorter, so the UK has winter.

questions.question: How long does Earth take to rotate once on its axis?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth rotates once in about 24 hours.

questions.question: How long does Earth take to orbit the Sun?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth takes about 365.25 days to orbit the Sun.

questions.question: What mainly causes seasons in the UK?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth's tilted axis mainly causes seasons.

questions.question: Why does the UK have summer when the northern hemisphere is tilted towards the Sun?
questions.modelAnswer: The UK gets more direct sunlight and longer daylight hours, so more energy reaches the ground.

questions.question: Give evidence from the source against the distance-from-Sun misconception.
questions.modelAnswer: If distance were the main cause, both hemispheres would have the same season; also the northern hemisphere has winter when Earth is near its closest point to the Sun.

data.sourcePassage: The Moon is Earth's natural satellite. It does not make its own light; we see it because it reflects sunlight. At most times, half of the Moon is lit by the Sun. As the Moon orbits Earth, observers see different amounts of this sunlit half, producing the phases of the Moon. The cycle from one new Moon to the next takes about 29.5 days. Moon phases are not usually caused by Earth's shadow. Earth's shadow causes a lunar eclipse only when the Sun, Earth and Moon line up in a special way. A solar eclipse happens when the Moon moves between the Sun and Earth.

questions.question: Why can we see the Moon?
questions.modelAnswer: We see the Moon because it reflects sunlight.

questions.question: How long is the Moon phase cycle from one new Moon to the next?
questions.modelAnswer: It takes about 29.5 days.

questions.question: What causes normal Moon phases?
questions.modelAnswer: They are caused by our changing view of the Moon's sunlit half.
acceptedKeywords: Our changing view of the Moon's sunlit half
options: Our changing view of the Moon's sunlit half

questions.question: What is the difference between a solar eclipse and a lunar eclipse?
questions.modelAnswer: A solar eclipse happens when the Moon blocks sunlight from Earth; a lunar eclipse happens when Earth's shadow falls on the Moon.

questions.question: Why do eclipses not happen every month?
questions.modelAnswer: The Moon's orbit is tilted compared with Earth's orbit, so the Sun, Earth and Moon usually do not line up exactly.

data.sourcePassage: A satellite is any object that orbits another object. Natural satellites form naturally, such as the Moon. Artificial satellites are made by humans and placed into orbit. They are used for communication, GPS navigation, weather forecasting, Earth observation and science. Low Earth orbit satellites move quickly over the ground, while geostationary satellites orbit once per day above Earth's equator and appear to stay over the same place. Space exploration also uses telescopes, probes, orbiters, landers, rovers, crewed missions and space stations. Robotic missions are usually safer and cheaper, but crewed missions can be more flexible because astronauts can make decisions and repair equipment.

questions.question: Give one example of a natural satellite.
questions.modelAnswer: Earth's Moon is a natural satellite.

questions.question: Give two uses of artificial satellites.
questions.modelAnswer: Artificial satellites can be used for communication, GPS navigation, weather forecasting, Earth observation or science.

questions.question: Why are geostationary satellites useful for communication?
questions.modelAnswer: They appear to stay above the same part of Earth, so dishes can point in one direction.
acceptedKeywords: They appear to stay over the same place
options: They appear to stay over the same place

questions.question: Compare robotic and crewed missions using one benefit of each.
questions.modelAnswer: Robotic missions are safer and cheaper because humans are not put at risk, while crewed missions can be more flexible because astronauts can make decisions and repair equipment.

questions.question: Name one risk or limitation of space exploration.
questions.modelAnswer: Risks and limitations include high cost, launch risks, radiation, life support needs, communication delay, fuel limits, space debris and possible contamination.

data.sourcePassage: Space is so large that diagrams are often not to scale. A diagram may show the order of planets clearly but fail to show true sizes and distances at the same time. A light-year is a unit of distance, not time. In a scale calculation, if 1 cm represents 50 million km, Earth at 150 million km from the Sun would be 3 cm from the Sun on the model. Scientists also use models to test ideas, such as using a lamp and paper to investigate sunlight angle. In that investigation, the independent variable is the angle of light and the dependent variable is the size or brightness of the patch. Repeats help identify anomalies and calculate a more trustworthy mean.

questions.question: What is a light-year a unit of?
questions.modelAnswer: A light-year is a unit of distance.

questions.question: Using the scale 1 cm represents 50 million km, how far would Earth be from the Sun if its real distance is 150 million km?
questions.modelAnswer: Earth would be 3 cm from the Sun because 150 divided by 50 is 3.

questions.question: In the sunlight angle investigation, what is the independent variable?
questions.modelAnswer: The independent variable is the angle of light.

questions.question: Give one strength and one limitation of a Solar System model.
questions.modelAnswer: A strength is that it can show order or relative size; a limitation is that it usually cannot show true size and true distance together.

questions.question: Why are repeat readings useful in an investigation?
questions.modelAnswer: Repeat readings improve reliability by helping identify anomalous results and allowing a more trustworthy mean to be calculated.
